explain.say: Bluetooth is a short-range radio working at 2.4 gigahertz. When you put headphones into pairing mode, they keep sending small advertising messages saying their name and what kind of device they are.

explain.say: Each device picks secret numbers and uses clever maths to agree on a shared key without ever sending the key itself, so an eavesdropper cannot work it out. Devices with screens may show a six-digit code for you to check matches.

faq.a: It makes a device discoverable: it repeatedly broadcasts short messages with its name and type so phones and computers nearby can find it. Outside pairing mode, devices usually only answer gadgets they already know.
asks: Why do I have to hold the button to pair headphones?

faq.q: How does Bluetooth keep my data private?
faq.a: During pairing the two devices use a key-exchange method that lets them agree on a shared secret key without sending it. Everything after that is encrypted with the key, so others nearby cannot understand it.

faq.q: Why do I sometimes have to confirm a code?
faq.a: Showing the same six-digit number on both screens proves you are pairing with the right device and that nobody has slipped in between. Simple gadgets without screens, like earbuds, skip this step.
asks: What is the Bluetooth pairing code for?

faq.q: Why do paired devices reconnect automatically?
faq.a: After pairing, both devices save the shared key, which is called bonding. When they meet again, they recognise each other's key and connect without asking you.
Most phones and headphones work up to about 10 metres, less through walls or your body. Bluetooth uses low power on purpose to save batteries.
asks: What is the range of Bluetooth?

facts: Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united Danish tribes.
Classic Bluetooth hops among 79 radio channels about 1,600 times a second.
